items.prompt: Why is skin built from two distinct layers rather than being a single sheet of tissue?

options.label: One layer handles cold weather, the other handles hot weather
options.feedback: Neither layer is dedicated to a particular temperature; both stay in place year-round and work together at every temperature.

options.label: The outer layer protects and seals, while the layer beneath supplies and repairs it
options.feedback: The tough outer layer forms a protective seal, while the living layer underneath supplies it with blood, nerves and the fresh cells it needs to keep working.

options.label: Splitting skin into layers makes it easier to see through in dim light
options.feedback: Seeing through skin plays no part in why it is layered; the layering exists for protection and support, not for transparency.

options.label: The two layers allow skin to be replaced all at once when damaged
options.feedback: Skin is not swapped out as a whole after damage; it renews itself gradually and continuously from within its lower layer instead.

items.ok_title: A seal on top of a supply line
items.ok_line: One layer guards the surface, the other keeps it fed.
items.ko_title: Not the reason for two layers
items.ko_line: Think about what a tough outer seal needs, that it cannot supply for itself.
items.exp_title: A seal with its own supply line
items.exp_text: The outer layer of skin is made of tightly packed, tough cells that form a protective seal against the outside world, but that layer has no blood vessels running through it to keep it nourished. Underneath sits a thicker layer threaded with blood vessels and nerves, which feeds fresh cells upward to replace the outer layer as it wears away. Skin needs both: a barrier layer facing outward, and a living layer behind it doing the work of keeping that barrier supplied.

items.prompt: Why are the cells right at the very surface of your skin already dead?

options.label: The body deliberately poisons its outermost cells to stop infection
options.feedback: Nothing about the process involves poisoning cells; they die naturally as they harden and move away from their blood supply, not from any deliberate attack.

options.label: Sunlight kills skin cells as soon as they reach the surface
options.feedback: The dying of these surface cells happens as a normal part of their journey upward from the living layer, whether or not sunlight ever reaches them.

options.label: Cells rise from the living layer below, hardening and dying as they near the surface
options.feedback: As cells move upward and away from their blood supply, they fill with a tough protein and die, ending up as a hardened, protective layer at the surface.

options.label: Friction from clothing wears the living cells down until they die
options.feedback: This layer of dead cells forms even on skin that is never touched by clothing at all, so friction is not what causes it.

items.ok_line: The cells at the surface finished their journey up from the living layer below.
items.ko_line: This happens everywhere on the body, touched by clothing or not, sunlit or not.
items.exp_title: A journey that ends in hardening
items.exp_text: New skin cells are constantly produced in the living layer beneath the surface, and as older cells are pushed upward by the ones forming behind them, they gradually fill with a tough, fibrous protein and lose their blood supply. By the time a cell reaches the outer surface, it has hardened completely and is no longer alive. What is touched, and eventually flakes away, is this outermost layer of cells that have already finished their working life.

items.prompt: What makes skin an effective waterproof barrier?

options.label: A layer of trapped air held just beneath the surface
options.feedback: There is no cushion of trapped air under the skin acting as a barrier; the waterproofing comes from the structure of the cells themselves.

options.label: An oily film sprayed continuously across the whole surface
options.feedback: While skin does carry some natural oils, the barrier itself is the structure of the outer layer's cells, not a continuous spray of oil across it.

options.label: Tiny scales that overlap like roof tiles to shed water
options.feedback: Human skin is not made of overlapping scales; its water resistance comes from the dense, protein-packed layer of flattened cells at its surface.

options.label: A dense layer of tough, flattened cells packed with a water-resistant protein
options.feedback: The outer layer's cells are flattened, tightly packed and filled with a fibrous protein that water struggles to pass through, sealing the surface.

items.ok_line: Flattened cells, packed tight and filled with a tough protein, are what keep water out.
items.ko_line: The barrier comes from the structure of the cells at the surface, not from anything added on top of them.
items.exp_title: A barrier built from packed, hardened cells
items.exp_text: The outermost layer of skin is made of flattened, overlapping cells packed tightly together and filled almost entirely with a tough, fibrous protein that water does not easily pass through. Because those cells overlap and interlock, there are very few gaps for water to slip through in either direction. That dense arrangement is what lets skin hold moisture in on the inside while keeping water on the outside from soaking through.

items.prompt: Why does sweating cool the body down?

options.label: Sweat reflects sunlight away from the skin
options.feedback: Cooling by sweat has nothing to do with reflecting light; it works by drawing heat away as the liquid evaporates, sunny or not.

options.label: Sweat is naturally cold when it reaches the skin's surface
options.feedback: Sweat is produced at body temperature; it is not cold to begin with, and the cooling effect comes from evaporation, not from the sweat's own temperature.

options.label: Sweat washes heat off the skin as it drips away
options.feedback: Sweat that simply drips off the skin without evaporating carries very little heat away with it; the real cooling comes from sweat turning into vapour.

options.label: Turning sweat into vapour on the skin draws heat away from the body
options.feedback: Turning liquid sweat into vapour takes energy, and that energy is pulled from the skin as heat, which is why the skin feels cooler once sweat evaporates.

items.ok_line: Turning a liquid into vapour takes energy, and that energy comes out of the skin as heat.
items.ko_line: The cooling comes from sweat changing from liquid to vapour, not from the sweat's own temperature.
items.exp_text: Turning a liquid into vapour takes energy, since the molecules of the liquid have to be given enough energy to break free into the air. When sweat evaporates from the surface of the skin, it draws that needed energy from the skin itself, in the form of heat. As heat leaves the skin to power that change of state, the skin is left measurably cooler than before the sweat evaporated.

items.prompt: What is actually happening in the skin when goosebumps appear?

options.label: Tiny muscles at the base of each hair contract and pull it upright
options.feedback: A small muscle attached to the base of each hair follicle contracts, tugging the hair upright and puckering the skin around it into a small bump.

options.label: Blood rushes to the surface of the skin and swells it slightly
options.feedback: Goosebumps are caused by muscle contraction around each hair follicle, not by extra blood pooling at the skin's surface.

options.label: Sweat glands briefly close and bulge outward
options.feedback: Sweat glands are not involved in producing this reaction; the bumps come from tiny muscles pulling on the hairs themselves.

options.label: The outer layer of skin cells contracts across the whole body at once
options.feedback: The outer layer of skin is made of dead cells and cannot contract; the pulling is done by small living muscles beneath the surface, each acting on a single hair.

items.ok_line: Each hair has its own small muscle, and goosebumps appear when they all contract together.
items.ko_line: The bump around each hair is caused by a muscle contracting, not by blood or sweat glands.
items.exp_text: Every hair on the skin is anchored in a small pit called a follicle, and attached to the side of each follicle is a tiny muscle. When that muscle contracts, it tugs the hair upright and, in doing so, puckers the skin immediately around the follicle into a small raised bump. Goosebumps appear across a stretch of skin simply because many of these tiny muscles are contracting at the same moment, one bump for every hair pulled upright.

items.prompt: What is a single strand of hair actually made of?

options.label: A thin tube of solidified oil from the skin's glands
options.feedback: Oil from glands near the hair follicle coats the strand's surface, but the strand itself is built from hardened, protein-packed cells, not from solidified oil.

options.label: A living tissue that stays alive along its entire length
options.feedback: Only the very root of a hair, hidden below the skin's surface, is alive; the strand extending outward from it is made of cells that have already died.

options.label: Dead cells packed tightly with a tough structural protein
options.feedback: Once a hair cell rises away from its living root, it fills with a tough fibrous protein and dies, and the strand you see is built entirely from cells in that hardened state.

options.label: Fine strands of the same mineral found in bone
options.feedback: Hair is not built from the mineral that gives bone its hardness; it is made of a different, fibrous protein entirely, produced by cells at the hair's root.

items.ok_line: What grows out of the follicle is already dead, hardened cell by cell as it forms.
items.ko_title: Not what a hair is made of
items.ko_line: Only the very base of a hair, hidden under the skin, is living tissue.
items.exp_title: A strand built from cells already dead
items.exp_text: A hair grows from a small cluster of living cells at its root, tucked below the surface of the skin, and this root is the only living part of the whole structure. As new cells are produced there, older cells are pushed upward and away from the root, filling with a tough structural protein and dying in the process, much as skin cells do on their way to the surface. The strand of hair that extends out from the skin is entirely made of these hardened, dead cells stacked end to end.

items.prompt: Why does cutting hair or trimming nails not hurt, even though cutting skin does?

options.label: Both are made of hardened, dead material with no nerve endings running through them
options.feedback: Nerve endings sit in the living skin at the root of a hair or the base of a nail, not in the hardened material extending out from it, so cutting that material feels nothing.

options.label: Hair and nails are numbed by natural oils that coat them
options.feedback: Any oil on hair or nails sits on their surface and has no numbing effect; the reason cutting them does not hurt is that they contain no living nerve tissue at all.

options.label: The body releases a painkiller automatically whenever hair or nails are cut
options.feedback: No painkiller is released for this; there is simply nothing to feel pain with in the parts of hair or nail that get cut.

options.label: Hair and nails grow too slowly for nerves to reach them
options.feedback: Growth speed is not the issue; hair and nails do not hurt when cut because the visible parts contain no living nerve tissue at all, regardless of how quickly they grow.

items.ok_line: The part being cut is already dead material, with no nerves running through it.
items.ko_line: Ask where the nerve endings actually sit, and how far the blade is from them.
items.exp_title: Cutting material with nothing left to feel
items.exp_text: Nerve endings that can register pain are found in the living skin, including the living root of a hair follicle or the base where a nail grows from. The visible length of a hair, and the outer part of a nail that gets trimmed, are both made of hardened, dead material extending outward from those living roots. A blade passing through that outward length never reaches any nerve tissue, which is exactly why the cutting goes unfelt.

items.prompt: Why are nails flat and rigid while hair is thin and flexible, even though both are built from the same kind of protein?

options.label: The protein is arranged in dense, flat sheets in a nail and in fine, round strands in hair
options.feedback: Packed into broad, layered sheets, the same protein forms a rigid plate; wound into a fine, round strand instead, it becomes flexible.

options.label: Nails contain a harder version of the protein than hair does
options.feedback: The material inside a nail and a hair is essentially the same protein; the difference in rigidity comes from how it is arranged, not from a different, harder version of it.

options.label: Nails are kept rigid by a mineral coating similar to that in bone
options.feedback: Nails are not coated in bone mineral; their stiffness comes purely from how the same protein found in hair is packed and layered.

options.label: Hair stays flexible because it never fully hardens like a nail does
options.feedback: Hair does fully harden as it forms, the same as a nail; it is flexible because of its thin, round shape, not because it stays soft.

items.ok_line: Layered flat, it forms a rigid plate; wound into a strand, the same protein flexes easily.
items.ko_title: Not the reason for the difference
items.ko_line: Both are built from the same protein; the difference has to come from how that protein is arranged.
items.exp_text: Hair and nails are both built from the same tough structural protein, produced by living cells at their roots and then left behind as those cells harden and die. In a nail, this protein is laid down in broad, densely packed, overlapping sheets that resist bending, forming a stiff, flat plate. In a hair, the same protein is instead wound into a fine, round strand, which can flex and bend along its length far more easily than a flat sheet ever could.

items.prompt: Why do the fine ridges on a fingertip help you grip something?

options.label: The ridges release a sticky substance that glues the finger to a surface
options.feedback: Nothing sticky is released from these ridges; their grip comes purely from the extra friction their raised pattern creates against a surface.

options.label: The ridges increase friction against a surface, especially once slightly damp
options.feedback: Raised ridges bite into a surface far more than flat skin would, and once dampened by sweat they grip even more firmly, the same way tyre treads work best on wet roads.

options.label: The ridges make the fingertip lighter so it presses more evenly
options.feedback: Weight has nothing to do with how these ridges help; the improved grip comes from increased friction, not from any change in how heavily the finger presses.

options.label: The ridges reflect light so the eyes can judge grip strength
options.feedback: Grip does not depend on how light bounces off the fingertip; the ridges work by physically increasing friction against whatever is being held.

items.ok_line: Raised ridges bite into a surface the way a tread bites into a wet road.
items.ko_line: Think about what a raised, textured surface does to the friction between two things pressed together.
items.exp_text: A flat, smooth surface slides against another surface fairly easily, while a surface broken up into fine ridges catches and resists sliding far more, since the raised ridges can press into tiny irregularities in whatever they touch. On a fingertip, this ridged pattern increases the friction between skin and an object, and the effect grows stronger once the ridges are lightly dampened, since a thin film of moisture helps the raised skin cling rather than slip. That extra resistance to sliding is what makes a ridged fingertip harder to lose grip with than smooth skin would be.

items.prompt: Why does hair fall out and get replaced gradually rather than the whole head shedding and regrowing all at once?

options.label: Hair only falls out when it is deliberately pulled or brushed
options.feedback: Hair sheds on its own as part of a natural cycle inside each follicle, whether or not it is ever touched, brushed, or pulled.

options.label: Each hair follicle cycles through growth and rest independently of the others
options.feedback: Every hair follicle runs through its own private cycle of active growth followed by a resting phase and shedding, out of step with the follicles around it.

options.label: The whole scalp regrows hair on a fixed yearly schedule
options.feedback: There is no single scalp-wide schedule that every follicle follows together; each one runs through its cycle on its own timing, independent of the others.

options.label: Only damaged hairs fall out, while healthy ones never do
options.feedback: Healthy hairs shed too, once their own follicle reaches the resting and shedding stage of its cycle, quite apart from any damage.

items.ok_line: Each follicle runs its own private cycle, so shedding never lines up across the whole head at once.
items.ko_line: Think about whether every follicle on the head is doing the same thing at the same time.
items.exp_text: Each hair follicle runs through a cycle of its own: a long phase of active growth, followed by a shorter resting phase, and finally the shedding of the old hair before the follicle starts growing a new one. Because every follicle on the head runs this cycle independently and starts at a different point in it, only a small share of follicles are shedding a hair at any given moment. That constant, staggered turnover is what lets hair fall out and regrow steadily, rather than the whole head shedding together and leaving it bare at once.
